title: A voice remembered as a goddess
subtitle: Andal · Goda · Kodai
caption: Andal and Krishna in a symbolic devotional composition. AI-generated illustration, not a historical scene.
paragraphs: Andal is revered in the Sri Vaishnava tradition as the only woman among the twelve Alvar poet-saints, and as Bhudevi, the earth goddess and consort of Vishnu ([temple tradition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Srivilliputhur_Andal_Temple)). The story told here follows that devotional remembrance, while keeping sacred narrative distinct from a documented modern biography.

The traditional accounts call her Kodai or Kothai, also known as Goda, and place her childhood at Srivilliputhur with her foster father Periyalvar, or Vishnuchitta ([traditional account](https://srivaishnavism.redzambala.com/sri-vaishnavism/nacciyar-tirumoli-andal.html)). Names and details vary between retellings; this version follows the central thread of her upbringing, garlands, poetry, longing, and union with Ranganatha.

title: The child in the tulasi garden
subtitle: A gift discovered among the flowers
caption: Periyalvar discovers the child near a tulasi plant in the traditional account. AI-generated devotional illustration.
paragraphs: According to the cherished account, Periyalvar found an infant girl beneath a tulasi plant while tending the garden and gathering flowers for Vishnu; he brought her home and raised her as his daughter ([traditional account](https://srivaishnavism.redzambala.com/sri-vaishnavism/nacciyar-tirumoli-andal.html)). The garden becomes the story's first meeting place between everyday care and divine grace.

Srivilliputhur's Aadi Pooram celebration continues to remember Periyalvar's adoption of Andal, with worship and a procession of Andal and Rangamannar ([Srivilliputhur Municipality](https://www.tnurbantree.tn.gov.in/srivilliputhur/places-of-interest/)). The living festival gives the found child's story a place in the shared memory of a community.

title: Growing among songs and garlands
subtitle: A household shaped by devotion
caption: A temple garden evokes the setting of Andal's upbringing. AI-generated illustration.
paragraphs: Periyalvar served Vishnu at Srivilliputhur by preparing flower and tulasi garlands, and the traditional narrative describes Goda helping him, visiting the temple, and growing deeply devoted to Krishna ([traditional account](https://srivaishnavism.redzambala.com/sri-vaishnavism/nacciyar-tirumoli-andal.html)). Devotion in this household is not only something spoken about: it takes the form of gathering, making, singing, and offering.

The temple is associated with Andal's Thiruppavai and Periyalvar's Tirupallandu, Tamil hymns that remain part of its worship ([Srivilliputhur Municipality](https://www.tnurbantree.tn.gov.in/srivilliputhur/places-of-interest/)). Their remembered relationship joins two poetic voices without making them the same: the father's protective affection and the daughter's insistent love have different emotional worlds.

title: The garland she wore first
subtitle: Love before offering
caption: Andal tries on a garland intended for Vishnu, as told in the devotional tradition. AI-generated illustration.
paragraphs: In the best-known episode of her life, Goda secretly wore the garlands prepared for the deity and looked at herself in a mirror, imagining herself as the Lord's bride; she then returned the flowers for the temple offering ([traditional account](https://srivaishnavism.redzambala.com/sri-vaishnavism/nacciyar-tirumoli-andal.html)). The story presents this as an intimate act of devotion rather than an attempt to claim the offering for herself.

When Periyalvar discovered what she had done, he was distressed that a garland intended for the deity had already been worn, and he prepared another one ([temple tradition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Srivilliputhur_Andal_Temple)). Here the story sets the care of ritual preparation beside a devotion too immediate to understand itself as distant from its beloved.

title: The Lord asks for her flowers
subtitle: The offering transformed by love
caption: Flowers and devotion recall the garland accepted in the traditional dream account. AI-generated illustration.
paragraphs: The tradition tells that Vishnu appeared to Periyalvar in a dream and asked for the garlands Goda had worn, revealing that her loving touch was welcome rather than a defilement ([traditional account](https://srivaishnavism.redzambala.com/sri-vaishnavism/nacciyar-tirumoli-andal.html)). The father's understanding changes: the child's unexpected act is recognized as an offering of love.

Andal is remembered as Chudikodutha Sudarkodi, the radiant woman who wore and then offered the garland; garlands associated with her shrine continue to be sent to other Vishnu temples ([temple tradition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Srivilliputhur_Andal_Temple)). A simple string of flowers becomes the enduring emblem of a devotion that is personal, embodied, and accepted.

title: Thirty mornings with her companions
subtitle: The world of Thiruppavai
caption: A poetic visualization of companions gathering at dawn in Thiruppavai. AI-generated illustration.
paragraphs: Andal's Thiruppavai is a work of thirty pasurams, while the longer Nachiyar Tirumoli is her other principal collection; both are treasured as expressions of refuge in Vishnu ([traditional account of the works](https://srivaishnavism.redzambala.com/sri-vaishnavism/nacciyar-tirumoli-andal.html)). This app's reading journey follows the thirty verses rather than treating them as episodes from a literal diary.

In the poems, a speaking voice calls companions to a shared observance, wakes sleepers, praises Krishna, approaches his household, and finally asks for lasting service and devotion ([Tamil text](https://tamilnation.org/sathyam/east/pirapantam/mp005baandaal)). Their movement can be read as a journey from gathering together to understanding what the heart truly seeks.

title: Longing and the wedding dream
subtitle: Nachiyar Tirumoli · Varanam Ayiram
caption: A symbolic bridal procession evokes the wedding dream, not a documentary reconstruction. AI-generated illustration.
paragraphs: The sixth sequence of Nachiyar Tirumoli, known as Varanam Ayiram, describes Andal dreaming of marriage to Narayana through ceremonial preparations, blessings, joining hands, and offerings at the sacred fire ([literary discussion](https://poetryatsangam.com/2018/08/i-dreamt-this-dream-my-friend-varanam-aayiram-by-ravi-shankar/)). It is a poem of dream and longing, and should not be mistaken for an eyewitness report of a human wedding.

The sequence continues to have a place in Tamil Vaishnava marriage traditions ([literary discussion](https://poetryatsangam.com/2018/08/i-dreamt-this-dream-my-friend-varanam-aayiram-by-ravi-shankar/)). In this way a deeply individual poetic voice becomes part of other people's shared hopes, rituals, and promises.

title: The journey to Srirangam
subtitle: Her chosen beloved
caption: Andal's palanquin journey toward Srirangam, following the devotional narrative. AI-generated illustration.
paragraphs: When marriage was discussed, the traditional account says Andal would accept only the Lord, and identifies Ranganatha of Srirangam as her chosen beloved; it then tells of divine instructions received in dreams to bring her to his temple ([traditional account](https://srivaishnavism.redzambala.com/sri-vaishnavism/nacciyar-tirumoli-andal.html)). The narrative gives outward movement to the inward direction her life has already taken.

The journey is described as a procession with a palanquin, flowers, attendants, and temple honours, with Periyalvar accompanying her to Srirangam ([traditional account](https://srivaishnavism.redzambala.com/sri-vaishnavism/nacciyar-tirumoli-andal.html)). Different retellings adorn the procession differently; its central meaning is the daughter's unwavering devotion and the father's loving accompaniment.

title: Union with Ranganatha
subtitle: The culmination of the sacred story
caption: Andal approaches the radiance of Ranganatha's sanctum. Symbolic AI-generated devotional illustration.
paragraphs: At Srirangam, the devotional account culminates in Andal entering Ranganatha's sanctuary and attaining union with him; one retelling describes her merging into divine light before the reclining Lord ([traditional account](https://srivaishnavism.redzambala.com/sri-vaishnavism/nacciyar-tirumoli-andal.html)). This is presented here as a sacred belief, not as a historically demonstrable physical event.

The Srivilliputhur temple tradition also remembers her marriage to Ranganatha and reveres her with Rangamannar ([temple account](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Srivilliputhur_Andal_Temple)). For the devotional reader, the ending answers the longing that has run through the story from garden to garland to song.

title: The garland continues
subtitle: A living poetic and devotional legacy
caption: Andal's garland and Krishna's flute symbolize enduring devotion. AI-generated illustration.
paragraphs: At Srivilliputhur, Andal's hymns remain part of daily worship and the Aadi Pooram festival continues to draw devotees in celebration of her remembered life ([Srivilliputhur Municipality](https://www.tnurbantree.tn.gov.in/srivilliputhur/places-of-interest/)). The story has not survived only as a written account; it is renewed in voices, flowers, music, and gatherings.

Her verses are especially associated with Margazhi recitation, and the temple's garland traditions connect her shrine to other places of Vishnu worship ([temple tradition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Srivilliputhur_Andal_Temple)). Returning to one pasuram at a time offers a simple way to encounter that legacy: not by rushing through the story, but by allowing its words to become familiar.
